senses.gloss: The arrival of a large number of unwanted people or things in a place.
examples: Every June the town braces for an *invasion* of tourists.
We had an *invasion* of ants in the kitchen after the rain.
Shop owners complained about the summer *invasion* of college kids.

senses.gloss: An act of interfering with someone's privacy or personal rights.
examples: She sued the magazine for *invasion* of privacy.
Reading someone's texts is a serious *invasion* of privacy.
Employees saw the tracking software as an *invasion*.

senses.gloss: Something made up that is not true.
examples: His account of that night was pure *invention*.
The detective decided the alibi was an *invention*.
Half of what he says about his past is *invention*.

senses.gloss: A complete list of the things in a place.
examples: The manager took an *inventory* of everything in the storeroom.
We keep an *inventory* of the tools in each truck.
The insurance company asked for an *inventory* of the damaged items.

senses.gloss: A layer of warm air that traps cooler air and smog near the ground.
examples: An *inversion* held the smoke over the valley for a week.
Air quality drops whenever a winter *inversion* settles in.
The forecast calls for an *inversion* through Thursday.

senses.gloss: Something that makes an unwanted result likely.
examples: Leaving a laptop on the seat is an *invitation* to thieves.
An unlocked garage is just an *invitation* for trouble.
Those loose wires are an *invitation* to a fire.

senses.gloss: Soreness or redness where something has rubbed or stung the skin.
examples: The new detergent caused *irritation* on her hands.
Wearing the mask all day led to some skin *irritation*.
These drops relieve *irritation* in dry eyes.

senses.gloss: A place where two things are joined.
examples: The leak was at the *juncture* of the two pipes.
A crack ran along the *juncture* of the wall and the ceiling.
The town sits at the *juncture* of two rivers.

senses.gloss: A good reason showing that an action was right or necessary.
examples: There was no *justification* for shouting at the clerk.
The memo offered a detailed *justification* for the budget cut.
He gave a long *justification* of his decision to quit.

senses.gloss: A constantly changing mixture of colors, people, or events.
examples: The market was a *kaleidoscope* of colors and smells.
The novel gives us a *kaleidoscope* of New York voices.
Her first year abroad was a *kaleidoscope* of new experiences.

senses.gloss: The row of keys on a piano or organ, or an electronic instrument with them.
examples: She bought a used *keyboard* to practice on at home.
He plays guitar, and his sister plays *keyboards* in the band.
His hands moved easily across the *keyboard* of the old piano.

senses.gloss: The part of something that everything else depends on.
examples: Trust is the *keystone* of any partnership.
The tax credit was the *keystone* of the whole plan.
Reading is the *keystone* of the early curriculum.

senses.gloss: A sudden backward jerk of a power tool when the blade catches.
examples: Hold the saw with both hands to control the *kickback*.
*Kickback* causes most chainsaw injuries.
The blade guard is there to reduce *kickback*.

senses.gloss: An extremely attractive person.
examples: She looked like a *knockout* in that dress.
Their new singer is an absolute *knockout*.
Everyone told him his date was a *knockout*.

senses.gloss: An event or achievement that marks an important stage.
examples: The vaccine was a *landmark* in modern medicine.
The ruling is considered a *landmark* in civil rights law.
Her first novel was a *landmark* for writers of her generation.

senses.gloss: The whole set of conditions in an area of activity at a given time.
examples: Streaming changed the *landscape* of the music business.
The political *landscape* looks very different after the election.
Small firms have to survive in a crowded competitive *landscape*.

senses.gloss: A painting or photograph of country scenery.
examples: A small *landscape* hung above the fireplace.
The museum's *landscapes* are mostly from the 1800s.
He paints *landscapes* of the Hudson Valley.

senses.gloss: The page format that is wider than it is tall.
examples: Print the spreadsheet in *landscape* so the columns fit.
Switch the page to *landscape* before you add the chart.
The photo works better in *landscape* than in portrait.

senses.gloss: An election win by an enormous margin.
examples: The governor was reelected in a *landslide*.
Early returns already pointed to a *landslide*.
She won the student council race by a *landslide*.

senses.gloss: Freedom to choose how to act or what to do.
examples: Teachers here are given a lot of *latitude* in the classroom.
The contract allows some *latitude* on the deadline.
Judges have considerable *latitude* in sentencing.

senses.gloss: The washing of clothes, sheets, and towels.
examples: The contract covers *laundering* of all the table linens.
Frequent *laundering* faded the color out of the shirt.
The label warns that *laundering* may shrink the fabric.

senses.gloss: A pale purple color.
examples: The bedroom walls were painted a soft *lavender*.
She chose *lavender* for the bridesmaids' dresses.
The sky turned *lavender* just after sunset.

senses.gloss: The people who lead an organization, taken together.
examples: The union's *leadership* voted to accept the offer.
Party *leadership* met behind closed doors.
New *leadership* took over the company last spring.

senses.gloss: Deep knowledge gained through years of study.
examples: He was a man of great *learning* and great modesty.
The library holds centuries of *learning*.
She wore her *learning* lightly and never showed off.

senses.gloss: The extra force you get by pushing on a bar or handle.
examples: Use a longer wrench for more *leverage*.
He couldn't get enough *leverage* to pry the lid off.
Up on the ladder, she had no *leverage* at all.

senses.gloss: Borrowed money used to increase the possible return on an investment.
examples: The firm took on too much *leverage* before the crash.
High *leverage* magnifies both gains and losses.
The fund cut its *leverage* in half after a bad quarter.

senses.gloss: Legal responsibility for damage, injury, or loss.
examples: The company denies any *liability* for the accident.
Every contractor here has to carry *liability* insurance.
The waiver limits the gym's *liability*.

senses.gloss: A person or thing that causes trouble or puts you at a disadvantage.
examples: With that temper, he's a *liability* to the team.
The old boiler has become a real *liability*.
Not having a driver's license turned out to be a *liability*.

senses.gloss: A trusted assistant who carries out a leader's orders.
examples: The mayor sent one of his *lieutenants* to the meeting.
She was the senator's chief *lieutenant* for twenty years.
The boss and his *lieutenants* ran the whole operation.

senses.gloss: Something that provides essential help or keeps something going.
examples: The loan was a *lifeline* for the family business.
The ferry is the island's only *lifeline* in winter.
For a lot of seniors, that daily call is a *lifeline*.

senses.gloss: A cord or thread tied tightly around something, especially a blood vessel in surgery.
examples: The surgeon placed a *ligature* around the artery.
The *ligature* slipped and the bleeding started again.
Police found *ligature* marks on the victim's wrists.

senses.gloss: How pale or bright a color is.
examples: Adjust the *lightness* of the image until the text is readable.
The two paints differ only in *lightness*.
She liked the *lightness* of the oak floor against the dark walls.

senses.gloss: Someone who speaks several languages well.
examples: He's a gifted *linguist* and picks up new languages fast.
The team hired a *linguist* to interpret at the meetings.
You don't have to be a *linguist* to get around Rome.
